meta.name: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS)
meta.notes: [bulk-tag pass: added `cks` tag to 61 questions] [cks batch 1: 13 balanced rewrites — recall=0] | 2026-07-20 hardening pass v1 [scheduled-agent]: full rewrite of all 61 single-answer + 1 multi-answer questions — removed 14 truncated options and 5 embedded self-rebuttal clauses inherited from prior automated passes, rebalanced correct-answer positions to 15/15/15/15 across A/B/C/D, brought correct==longest down from unmeasured to 26% (near random baseline) and correct==shortest to 35% via realistic technical padding on shorter distractors, and rewrote every explanation to state both why the correct answer is right AND why each distractor is wrong (several explanations previously discussed unrelated topics).

questions.question: A NetworkPolicy in the `prod` namespace must allow ingress to the `web` pods only from pods that live in the same namespace, and drop all cross-namespace traffic. Which ingress `from` selector expresses that intent?
options: `from: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: prod}}, podSelector: {}}]`
`from: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 0.0.0.0/0, except: [10.0.0.0/8]}}]` on the ingress rule
`from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}}]` on the ingress rule
`from: [{namespaceSelector: {}}]` on the ingress rule
questions.explanation: The `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label is added automatically to every namespace by the NamespaceDefaultLabelName feature, so a `namespaceSelector` matching that label plus an empty `podSelector: {}` allows every pod inside `prod` and only inside `prod`. An `ipBlock` filters by pod IP CIDR and cannot express namespace identity — pods in other namespaces can share the CIDR. A `podSelector` alone matches pods across the *same* namespace as the policy only when no `namespaceSelector` is present, but here a matching pod in any other namespace with label `app: web` would be permitted — the wording asks the policy to be scoped by namespace explicitly. An empty `namespaceSelector: {}` matches every namespace, allowing all cross-namespace traffic — the opposite of the requirement.

questions.question: kube-bench flags `1.2.6 Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument is not set to AlwaysAllow` on the API server. Which change to `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` remediates the finding without disabling authentication?
options: Add `--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction` alongside the existing `AlwaysAllow` value
Replace `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow` with `--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC`
Add `--anonymous-auth=false` and keep `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow`
Replace `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow` with `--authorization-mode=ABAC` and point `--authorization-policy-file` at a JSON policy
questions.explanation: `Node,RBAC` is the production-recommended combination: the Node authorizer scopes what each kubelet may see and change to its own node/pods, and RBAC handles every other principal. `NodeRestriction` is an admission plugin — it runs after authorization and cannot replace the authorization decision, so `AlwaysAllow` would still permit every action. `--anonymous-auth` controls authentication (whether a request without credentials becomes `system:anonymous`), not authorization; leaving `AlwaysAllow` in place still authorises every authenticated request unconditionally. ABAC works, but it is legacy, file-driven, and CIS explicitly recommends RBAC — configuring ABAC also leaves you managing a static JSON policy file per API server, which is exactly what RBAC replaced.

questions.question: Pods in a cloud-hosted cluster must be blocked from reaching the instance-metadata service at 169.254.169.254 using only in-cluster Kubernetes objects (no cloud-side firewall). Which control fits?
options: Enable the Pod Security `restricted` profile on every namespace so `runAsNonRoot`, `capabilities.drop=[ALL]`, and `allowPrivilegeEscalation=false` are enforced on every pod
Set `hostNetwork: false` on every pod so the pod runs in its own network namespace with a distinct routing table that will exclude the node's link-local metadata route
Apply a default-deny egress NetworkPolicy and add an allow rule that whitelists everything except `169.254.169.254/32`
Configure `--cloud-provider=external` on every kubelet so the in-tree cloud provider is disabled and pods lose the ambient credentials needed to reach the metadata service
questions.explanation: NetworkPolicy egress can express IP-level deny with an `except` on the metadata address, keeping regular egress paths open. Pod Security Standards constrain the pod spec (privileged, capabilities, volumes) — they know nothing about destination IPs. `hostNetwork: false` merely prevents the pod from sharing the node's network namespace; the pod still has full outbound routing to 169.254.169.254 via its own interface. The `--cloud-provider` flag configures how the kubelet talks to the cloud API for node/volume lifecycle; it does not police workload egress.

questions.question: A kubeadm control-plane initialisation must include `k8s.example.com` in the API server certificate's Subject Alternative Name list so remote kubectl users hit the DNS name without TLS errors. Which `ClusterConfiguration` field ships that SAN?
options: `networking.dnsDomain: k8s.example.com`
`apiServer.advertiseAddress: k8s.example.com`
`controlPlaneEndpoint: k8s.example.com` on its own with no other field
`apiServer.certSANs: ["k8s.example.com"]`
questions.explanation: `apiServer.certSANs` is the documented list of extra names kubeadm bakes into the API server's serving certificate at init. `networking.dnsDomain` sets the cluster's internal service DNS suffix (`svc.cluster.local` by default) — unrelated to the apiserver's serving cert. `controlPlaneEndpoint` sets the shared LB name for HA control planes; it does add its hostname to the SAN automatically, but the question asks specifically which field adds an arbitrary SAN like `k8s.example.com`, and `controlPlaneEndpoint` also has to be a routable endpoint. `advertiseAddress` is the bind IP the apiserver reports to peers; it accepts an IP, not a hostname, and never touches the cert.

questions.question: An Ingress must terminate TLS for `store.example.com` using a certificate stored in a Kubernetes Secret. Which Secret type and Ingress reference are correct?
options: Secret type `kubernetes.io/tls` with keys `tls.crt` and `tls.key`, referenced from `spec.tls[].secretName`
Secret type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` with the PEM embedded in the JWT payload
Secret type `Opaque` with keys `certificate` and `privateKey`, referenced from `spec.tls[].secretName`
Secret type `kubernetes.io/tls` with keys `ca.crt` and `ca.key`, referenced from `spec.rules[].http.paths[].backend.tls`
questions.explanation: Ingress TLS termination requires a Secret typed `kubernetes.io/tls` with the fixed keys `tls.crt` and `tls.key`; the Ingress lists the Secret in `spec.tls[].secretName`. `Opaque` with custom key names is not recognised by Ingress controllers — the type check fails. `service-account-token` Secrets carry API JWTs, not X.509 material. `ca.crt` and `ca.key` name a certificate authority pair used for signing, and there is no `spec.rules[].http.paths[].backend.tls` field on Ingress — TLS is declared at `spec.tls[]`, not per backend.

questions.question: The CIS benchmark rule `Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false` must be applied on kube-apiserver. What is the direct effect of setting `--anonymous-auth=false`?
options: The insecure HTTP port on 8080 is closed and refuses new connections
Requests without credentials are rejected with HTTP 401 instead of being mapped to user `system:anonymous`
Every request must present a bearer token; client-certificate auth is disabled at the same time
The `system:unauthenticated` group is deleted and any ClusterRoleBinding referencing it becomes invalid
questions.explanation: With anonymous auth disabled, an incoming request that carries no credentials fails authentication and the API server returns 401 — it is never mapped to the `system:anonymous` identity. Closing the insecure port is `--insecure-port=0`, a separate (also deprecated) flag. Client-certificate auth is a distinct authenticator and stays enabled. `system:unauthenticated` is a built-in group name; nothing about the anonymous-auth flag removes it — bindings that reference it simply match no user because no request is ever mapped to it anymore.

questions.question: A developer's ServiceAccount `dev-sa` in the `dev` namespace must be able to `get` and `list` Pods in `dev` only. Which RBAC objects satisfy least privilege?
options: A ClusterRole with verbs `["get","list","watch"]` on pods, bound to `dev-sa` with a ClusterRoleBinding
A ClusterRole with verbs `["get","list"]` on pods, bound to `dev-sa` with a RoleBinding scoped to the `dev` namespace
A Role in `dev` with verbs `["get","list"]` on pods, bound to `dev-sa` with a RoleBinding in `dev`
A Role in `dev` with verbs `["*"]` on `["*"]`, bound to `dev-sa` with a RoleBinding in `dev`
questions.explanation: A namespaced Role plus a RoleBinding, restricted to the exact verbs and the `pods` resource, is the tightest scope Kubernetes offers — nothing outside `dev` is granted. Binding a ClusterRole with a ClusterRoleBinding grants the verbs cluster-wide across every namespace. Binding a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding does scope the grant to `dev`, but the CKS-preferred pattern for a single-namespace grant is a namespaced Role, keeping the object graph namespace-local. Granting `["*"]` on `["*"]` inside `dev` is massive over-privilege even within one namespace.

questions.question: A batch Job Pod does not need to call the Kubernetes API. What is the safest way to guarantee no ServiceAccount token is mounted into that Pod?
options: Delete the `default` ServiceAccount from the namespace so no token can be assigned
Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the `default` ServiceAccount object
Leave `serviceAccountName` unset in the Pod spec — an omitted name suppresses token mounting
Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` in the Pod spec itself
questions.explanation: Setting the field on the Pod spec is the most targeted control and always overrides any looser value on the ServiceAccount. Deleting the default SA is disruptive and Kubernetes recreates it via the ServiceAccount controller. Turning the flag off on the SA affects every workload that uses it, potentially breaking other pods. Omitting `serviceAccountName` still assigns `default` implicitly, and `default` normally has `automountServiceAccountToken: true`, so a token is still projected.

questions.question: Which built-in admission plugin restricts each kubelet's API operations to its own Node object and to Pods scheduled on that node?
options: NodeRestriction
PodSecurity
AlwaysPullImages
ResourceQuota
questions.explanation: `NodeRestriction` reads the identity presented by the kubelet (user in the `system:nodes` group with a matching node name) and denies writes to any Node or Pod that doesn't belong to it — the standard defence against a compromised node pivoting into peers. `PodSecurity` validates pod security-context settings; it says nothing about which kubelet performed the write. `AlwaysPullImages` mutates pod specs to re-pull images on every start. `ResourceQuota` caps aggregate resource use per namespace.

questions.question: A cluster admin is preparing to move control-plane nodes from v1.29 to v1.30 with kubeadm. Which command, run first on the primary control-plane node, previews the upgrade — validating component versions and printing recommended steps without changing anything?
options: `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data`
`kubeadm upgrade plan`
`kubeadm upgrade apply v1.30.0`
`apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.30.0-*`
questions.explanation: `kubeadm upgrade plan` dry-runs the upgrade: it checks the current versions of API server, controller-manager, scheduler, kubelet, and etcd, and prints the recommended target version with any warnings. `kubectl drain` empties a worker node's workloads — that happens later, per worker, once the control plane is upgraded. `kubeadm upgrade apply` performs the actual control-plane version bump; it must come after `plan`. Installing the new `kubeadm` binary is a prerequisite to running `apply`, but it changes host packages and is not the safe read-only preview step the question asks for.

questions.question: A microservice needs read access to ConfigMaps in namespace `config` AND list access to Deployments in namespace `app`. Which design honours least privilege?
options: Grant the built-in `view` ClusterRole to the SA via a ClusterRoleBinding — it already contains the two needed verbs
Create a single Role in `config` with rules for both resources — Kubernetes will apply it across matching namespaces
Create two Roles (one per namespace) with only the verbs each needs, and bind each with a RoleBinding in its own namespace
Create a ClusterRole covering both resources and bind it with a ClusterRoleBinding for simplicity
questions.explanation: The lowest-privilege construction is one namespaced Role per namespace, each granting only the verb+resource pair actually needed, each bound via a RoleBinding in the same namespace. The `view` ClusterRole is far broader than the requirement (it grants read on almost every namespaced resource in every namespace it's bound in). A Role is namespace-scoped by definition — a Role in `config` cannot grant permissions in `app`. A ClusterRoleBinding grants the verbs cluster-wide, exceeding scope.

questions.question: Compliance requires that every read of a Secret is logged with the full request AND response payloads. Which combination of audit `stage` and `level` provides that?
options: Stage `RequestReceived`, level `Metadata`
Stage `RequestReceived`, level `Request`
Stage `ResponseStarted`, level `Request`
Stage `ResponseComplete`, level `RequestResponse`
questions.explanation: `RequestResponse` is the highest audit level and captures both bodies; `ResponseComplete` is the stage after the response has been fully sent, so the response body is available to log. `Metadata` records who/what/when but drops the bodies — exactly what compliance is asking to see. `Request` records the request body only; the read's *response* (which carries the Secret data) is not logged. `ResponseStarted` fires when the response head is written and is only useful for long-lived watches/exec streams, not point-in-time reads.

questions.question: Which built-in Kubernetes admission controller — GA since v1.25 — enforces that Pods in a namespace cannot run with `privileged: true`?
options: PodSecurity, with the namespace labelled `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline` (or stricter)
SecurityContextDeny, enabled in the API server's admission plugin list
NodeRestriction, applied at the kubelet layer
ValidatingAdmissionWebhook, pointing to an in-tree Kubernetes webhook that ships with the API server
questions.explanation: `PodSecurity` implements the Pod Security Standards. The `baseline` profile prohibits privileged containers (as does the stricter `restricted`), and is activated by labelling the namespace with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline`. `SecurityContextDeny` was deprecated and removed — you cannot rely on it. `NodeRestriction` limits what a kubelet can write via the API; it has no visibility into pod security context values. `ValidatingAdmissionWebhook` is the generic hook mechanism — there is no in-tree webhook that ships with Kubernetes for this; you'd have to deploy an external policy engine.

questions.question: Which API replaces the legacy long-lived ServiceAccount Secret and issues audience-bound, time-limited tokens that are invalidated when the Pod is deleted?
options: The Kubernetes CertificateSigningRequests API used for kubelet bootstrap
The TokenRequest API, consumed by the kubelet through a projected volume mount
The BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume feature — a separate REST endpoint the pod calls
The TokenReview API called from inside the pod on each request
questions.explanation: The TokenRequest API mints projected tokens with a defined `expirationSeconds` and a specific audience; the kubelet drives it automatically when the pod uses a `serviceAccountToken` projected volume, and the token becomes invalid once the pod is gone. CertificateSigningRequests issue X.509 client certs (used by node bootstrap and kubectl), not JWTs. `BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume` names the projected-volume plumbing but is not itself a REST endpoint — it consumes TokenRequest under the hood. TokenReview is the *validator* side of the JWT — the API server calls it to check tokens presented to it — and is not what mints them.

questions.question: After setting `--anonymous-auth=false` on kube-apiserver, which specific class of requests is affected?
options: External OIDC users — the API server stops validating their JWTs against the configured issuer
Kubelets — the node client certificates issued by kubeadm are invalidated at the next reload
Requests arriving with no credentials — previously mapped to `system:anonymous`, now rejected with HTTP 401
In-cluster ServiceAccount pods — their projected JWTs no longer authenticate until re-issued
questions.explanation: The flag only touches the *anonymous* authenticator, which mapped credential-less requests to the `system:anonymous` identity. With it disabled, such requests are rejected outright. OIDC, x509, and service-account authenticators are independent and continue to work. Kubelet certs and SA JWTs both carry credentials, so they are not anonymous and are unaffected.

questions.question: An AppArmor profile named `no-write-etc` is already loaded on every worker node. Which Pod-spec field references it in Kubernetes v1.30+ (using the GA `securityContext.appArmorProfile` field)?
options: A cluster-scoped `AppArmorProfile` CRD referenced from `spec.securityContext.appArmorProfileRef`
`metadata.annotations: {container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>: localhost/no-write-etc}`
`spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities.add: ["apparmor:no-write-etc"]`
`spec.containers[].securityContext.appArmorProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: no-write-etc}`
questions.explanation: The stable field takes `type: Localhost` plus the profile name in `localhostProfile`, matching the profile already loaded by the node's AppArmor userspace. The `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>` annotation is the legacy pre-1.30 mechanism; it still works but is not the current field-based syntax. AppArmor is not a Linux capability — the `capabilities` list controls kernel capabilities, not LSM profiles. There is no upstream `AppArmorProfile` CRD; the type is a plain string embedded in the pod spec.

questions.question: A container must use the runtime's default seccomp profile via the stable Kubernetes field (v1.22+). Which `securityContext.seccompProfile` value is correct?
options: `type: RuntimeDefault`
`type: Unconfined`
`type: Localhost, localhostProfile: default.json`
`type: Default, profile: docker/default`
questions.explanation: `RuntimeDefault` tells the kubelet to attach whatever seccomp filter the container runtime ships as its default (a moderate deny-list). `Unconfined` explicitly disables seccomp — the exact opposite. `Localhost` requires a JSON profile physically present under the kubelet's seccomp root and named in `localhostProfile`, which is a valid pattern for custom profiles but does not mean 'runtime default'. `Default` is not a real `type` value — the accepted values are only `Unconfined`, `RuntimeDefault`, and `Localhost`.

questions.question: Which combination of node-level actions best aligns with the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark for worker nodes covering kubelet flags, kubeconfig/PKI file permissions, and the read-only kubelet port?
options: Enable the read-only port on 10255 so Prometheus can scrape without TLS, and set `--anonymous-auth=true` for scrape endpoints
Set `--anonymous-auth=false` and `--authorization-mode=Webhook` on kubelet, set 0600 on kubeconfig and PKI files, and disable the read-only port (`--read-only-port=0`)
Set world-readable permissions on kubeconfig and PKI files so SRE staff can inspect them during incidents
Run kubelet with `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow` and `--anonymous-auth=true` to simplify troubleshooting; leave the read-only port on 10255
questions.explanation: The CIS worker-node profile requires the kubelet to authenticate every caller, delegate authorization to the API server (`Webhook`), keep sensitive files at 0600, and close the unauthenticated read-only port. Enabling 10255 without TLS is the exact anti-pattern the benchmark disallows. World-readable PKI leaks the node's client key material. `AlwaysAllow` + anonymous is a wide-open kubelet — CIS calls both out explicitly.

questions.question: Which command permanently prevents the `dccp` kernel module from loading on a worker node across reboots?
options: `modprobe -r dccp` on the running node, then commit the state by writing the unloaded module list to `/etc/modules-load.d/exclude.conf`
`systemctl disable dccp.service` so the systemd unit that lazy-loads the DCCP kernel module at socket use is prevented from starting on boot
Add `blacklist dccp` to a file such as `/etc/modprobe.d/kubernetes-blacklist.conf`
Append `dccp` to `/etc/modules` — the file drives kernel-module policy at boot, and its exclusion list ships with a `denylist` prefix by convention
questions.explanation: `modprobe.d` files are read at boot by systemd and modprobe; a `blacklist` directive there is the durable mechanism. `modprobe -r` only unloads for the current uptime — the module can reload on demand. There is no `dccp.service` shipped with Linux, so `systemctl disable` has nothing to disable. `/etc/modules` is the *load-at-boot* list; adding a module there does the opposite of blacklisting.

questions.question: Which Kubernetes feature (stable in v1.30) reduces the blast radius of a container root escape by mapping the container's UID 0 to a high, unprivileged UID on the host?
options: Pod Security `restricted` profile forcing `runAsNonRoot: true`
Seccomp `RuntimeDefault` profile applied to every container in the pod
AppArmor `runtime/default` profile applied via annotations
Pod-spec user namespaces via `spec.hostUsers: false`
questions.explanation: `hostUsers: false` opts a pod into the Linux user namespace: the kubelet asks the runtime to allocate a distinct UID range (e.g., 100000+), and container UID 0 is mapped to that unprivileged host UID. Seccomp filters syscalls but does not change the effective UID a host sees. AppArmor is a mandatory-access-control LSM; it cannot renumber processes. `runAsNonRoot: true` blocks images that try to start as UID 0 inside the container — it doesn't touch the container-to-host UID mapping.

questions.question: A container must bind to TCP port 80 but should hold no other elevated privileges. Which `securityContext.capabilities` shape delivers least privilege?
options: `drop: ["ALL"]; add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]`
`add: ["ALL"]`
`drop: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]`
Leave capabilities unset and set `runAsUser: 0`
questions.explanation: Drop every capability first, then grant back only `NET_BIND_SERVICE`, which is the exact kernel capability needed to open a privileged port as a non-root user. `add: ["ALL"]` grants every capability — the direct opposite. Dropping `NET_BIND_SERVICE` blocks the very ability the app needs. Running as UID 0 to open port 80 satisfies the requirement but breaks the *no other elevated privileges* rule — root gets full capabilities by default.

questions.question: Which single `securityContext` field sets the Linux `no_new_privs` bit, so setuid/setgid binaries and file capabilities inside the container cannot escalate privileges?
options: `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`
`allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`
`runAsNonRoot: true`
`capabilities.drop: ["SETUID","SETGID"]`
questions.explanation: `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` is the direct wrapper around the Linux `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` process flag. `readOnlyRootFilesystem` prevents writes to the container FS but doesn't stop a pre-existing setuid binary from running with elevated bits. `runAsNonRoot` is about the initial user identity, not privilege inheritance. Dropping SETUID/SETGID stops the container from calling `setuid()`/`setgid()`, but a setuid *binary* elevates before those syscalls are reached — `no_new_privs` is the specific control that blocks that path.

questions.question: Which single `securityContext` setting most directly stops an attacker from installing extra tooling (curl, nc, backdoors) inside a compromised container?
options: `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`
`capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`
`readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`
`runAsNonRoot: true`
questions.explanation: A read-only root filesystem returns EROFS on every write, so an attacker cannot drop new binaries anywhere except explicit writable volumes. `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` blocks setuid escalation but the disk stays writable. Dropping all capabilities reduces what the process can do at the kernel boundary but a plain user with normal file permissions can still write to writable paths. `runAsNonRoot` picks a non-zero UID; that UID still owns its home and often the app's data dir, so writes proceed.

questions.question: Which single Pod-spec setting represents the highest privilege-escalation risk in production and should be blocked at admission?
options: `spec.hostNetwork: true`
`spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsUser: 0`
`spec.hostPID: true`
`spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged: true`
questions.explanation: `privileged: true` disables the container runtime's Linux namespace/cgroup/LSM restrictions and grants every capability — it is the closest a Kubernetes-configured container gets to running directly on the host. `hostNetwork` and `hostPID` open a specific namespace boundary each — serious, but not the same broad blast radius. Running as UID 0 inside an otherwise sandboxed container is worse than running as a non-root UID, but the container's other isolation (capabilities, seccomp, cgroups) is still in force.

questions.question: The `payments` namespace is labelled `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted`. A deployment is rejected because its image runs as root. Which fix keeps the enforcement in place and lets the pod through?
options: Add `runAsNonRoot: true` and `runAsUser: 1000` on the container `securityContext`, or rebuild the image with a non-root `USER` line
Delete the namespace's LimitRange object — LimitRanges default new pods' security context to `runAsNonRoot: true` and dropping the LimitRange removes that default
Add `privileged: true` on the container `securityContext` so the container's security profile is granted admin exemptions and bypasses the `restricted` non-root check
Change the namespace's enforce label from `restricted` to `baseline` so root pods are admitted while other privileged-container prohibitions remain in force
questions.explanation: The `restricted` standard requires a non-root UID; declaring one in `securityContext` (or setting `USER` in the Dockerfile) satisfies it without loosening the namespace policy. Downgrading to `baseline` weakens security — not a fix, a workaround. LimitRange caps CPU/memory, it has nothing to do with user identity. `privileged: true` is explicitly forbidden by both `baseline` and `restricted`, so it would make the rejection worse.

questions.question: You want to block pods that use the `:latest` image tag cluster-wide using OPA Gatekeeper. Which two resources must you author?
options: A `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` pointing at a Rego policy file mounted on the API server, plus a `PolicySource` object listing which paths are enforced cluster-wide
A `ConstraintTemplate` (defining the Rego logic) plus a `Constraint` (an instance targeting kinds and namespaces)
A single `Policy` object referencing Gatekeeper's built-in `no-latest-tag` template, with `parameters.excludedNamespaces` covering system namespaces that legitimately float on latest
A `ClusterRole` denying the `create` verb on pods with `image` containing `latest`
questions.explanation: Gatekeeper's model is: a `ConstraintTemplate` CRD defines the Rego and its input schema, and a `Constraint` (a CRD instance of that template) turns it on for specified kinds/namespaces. The `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` used by Gatekeeper is installed automatically at deploy time — you don't author it. There is no `Policy` object in vanilla Gatekeeper (that is Kyverno's type name). RBAC evaluates verb/resource, not the *contents* of a field like the image string.

questions.question: A Secret must never appear in `kubectl describe pod` output or in `/proc/<pid>/environ`. Which consumption pattern satisfies both?
options: Load it via `envFrom.secretRef` for convenience
Reference it via `env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef`, one value at a time
Mount the Secret as a projected volume file and have the app read it from disk
Convert it to a ConfigMap with `immutable: true` — ConfigMaps encrypt at rest by default
questions.explanation: Volume-mounted Secret files never appear in the pod's environment (`/proc/<pid>/environ`) and are not printed by `kubectl describe pod`; only the Secret name is shown. Both `env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef` and `envFrom.secretRef` place the resolved values into the process environment, where they are visible to anyone with `describe` rights or read access to `/proc`. ConfigMaps are not encrypted at rest by default (they inherit whatever EncryptionConfiguration is set for `configmaps`) and are not designed for secret data.

questions.question: A regulated workload needs stronger kernel isolation than the default runc container runtime. Which Kubernetes resource selects an alternative runtime such as gVisor or Kata Containers for a pod?
options: A PodDisruptionBudget attached to the pod's controller
Setting `spec.hostPID: false` and `spec.hostNetwork: false` on the pod
A `securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` combined with `privileged: false`
A `RuntimeClass` object, referenced by name from `spec.runtimeClassName` on the pod
questions.explanation: `RuntimeClass` names a runtime handler (`runsc` for gVisor, `kata` for Kata) that the container runtime — configured by the node — will select instead of the default. `PodDisruptionBudget` governs voluntary evictions; unrelated to runtime choice. Read-only root FS + non-privileged is good hygiene, but the same underlying kernel and runc process still run the workload. Turning off host namespaces is baseline pod isolation, again with the default runtime — no sandbox is added.

questions.question: You want `production` to REJECT non-compliant pods, `staging` to WARN, and `development` to log VIOLATIONS to the audit trail. Which set of namespace labels achieves that?
options: `production: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted`, `staging: pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=baseline`, `development: pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=baseline`
Enable the `PodSecurity` feature gate and set the mode on the pods themselves
A single ClusterPolicy specifying `enforce: restricted, warn: baseline, audit: baseline`
`production: pod-security.kubernetes.io/mode=enforce`, `staging: pod-security.kubernetes.io/mode=warn`, `development: pod-security.kubernetes.io/mode=audit`
questions.explanation: The label key encodes the *mode* (`enforce`, `warn`, `audit`) and the value is the *level* (`privileged`, `baseline`, `restricted`). Labels like `pod-security.kubernetes.io/mode=...` invent a non-existent `mode` key — the mode is part of the key, not the value. `PodSecurity` has been stable for many releases; nothing configures modes at the pod level. Vanilla Kubernetes has no `ClusterPolicy` type — that belongs to Kyverno.

questions.question: A CI job must scan `nginx:1.25` with Trivy for CRITICAL CVEs and fail the pipeline when any are found. Which command does that?
options: `trivy scan image=nginx:1.25 severity=CRITICAL fail=true`
`trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 nginx:1.25`
`trivy container nginx:1.25 --threshold CRITICAL --exit 1`
`trivy image nginx:1.25 --level CRITICAL --fail-on-critical`
questions.explanation: `trivy image` is the container-image scanner; `--severity` filters, and `--exit-code 1` makes Trivy exit non-zero when at least one matching finding is present, which fails the CI job. The other three use flags and subcommands that do not exist in Trivy: there is no `trivy scan` subcommand, no `--threshold`, no `--level`, and no `--fail-on-critical`.

questions.question: Given a containerd handler named `runsc` for gVisor, which YAML creates the RuntimeClass a pod can then reference?
options: `apiVersion: apps/v1` / `kind: RuntimeClass` / `spec.runtime: runsc`
`apiVersion: v1` / `kind: RuntimeClass` / top-level `handler: runsc`
`apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1` / `kind: RuntimeClass` / top-level `handler: runsc`
`apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1beta1` / `kind: RuntimeClass` / `spec.runtimeHandler: runsc`
questions.explanation: The stable API is `node.k8s.io/v1`, with `handler` at the root of the object (no nested `spec`). `apps/v1` hosts Deployments/StatefulSets/DaemonSets — not RuntimeClass. The core `v1` group doesn't contain RuntimeClass either. The `v1beta1` shape with `spec.runtimeHandler` is the older schema and was replaced by the stable v1 layout.

questions.question: You just labelled `prod` with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted` and several existing deployments break. What is the least-disruptive way to identify every violation before enforcing?
options: Change enforcement to `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged`
Set `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest` to test the newest built-in version
Move to `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline` for now
Switch to `pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted` — violations are logged but no pod is rejected
questions.explanation: `audit` is the non-blocking observability mode: violations are annotated on API objects and written to the audit log, no admission is rejected. Setting `enforce=privileged` disables the policy entirely — nothing is checked. `enforce=baseline` is a valid stepping stone but still rejects `baseline` violations, so it's not the least disruptive choice. `enforce-version` selects which Kubernetes version's rules to apply, not the enforcement mode.

questions.question: A leaked Secret's external value has been rotated at the third-party provider. What completes the remediation inside Kubernetes?
options: Delete the old Secret and recreate it with the new value; then `kubectl rollout restart` any Deployment that consumed it as environment variables
Set `immutable: true` on the existing Secret to prevent further tampering — the flag also invalidates the old token cached in running pods so they re-authenticate against the new value

`kubectl patch secret <name> --patch '{"data": null}'` to wipe the stored payload without deleting the object, so consumers keep their existing Secret reference and Kubernetes re-populates the payload from a backing store
Bump the Secret's `metadata.resourceVersion` field to force the kubelet's Secret watcher to fire an update event and re-sync all consumer pod mounts and env values
questions.explanation: Recreating the object with the new value is the only way to change its data. Deployments that read the Secret via `env`/`envFrom` bake values in at pod start, so a rolling restart is required; volume-mounted Secrets get refreshed automatically by the kubelet, no restart needed. `immutable: true` only prevents future edits — it doesn't rotate the value. Patching `data: null` corrupts the object; readers get empty strings. `resourceVersion` is a server-managed optimistic-lock field; clients cannot set it manually.

questions.question: How is at-rest encryption for Kubernetes Secrets in etcd enabled using the built-in mechanism?
options: Add the annotation `encryption: true` to each Secret manifest — kube-apiserver's built-in EncryptionAnnotationController honours the annotation and transparently AES-encrypts the entry before it reaches etcd
Write an `EncryptionConfiguration` listing the `secrets` resource with an `aescbc` or KMS provider, then start kube-apiserver with `--encryption-provider-config=<path>`
Set `etcd.dataEncryption: true` in the kubeadm `ClusterConfiguration` under `etcd.local` so etcd generates a data-key on init and encrypts its own on-disk pages before the API server sees them
Set `--allow-privileged=false` on kube-apiserver so the process runs in a hardened profile that implicitly enables the EncryptionAtRest feature gate for `secrets` and `configmaps`
questions.explanation: The API server (not etcd itself) performs the encryption; you point it at an `EncryptionConfiguration` file with the desired provider (`aescbc`, `aesgcm`, `secretbox`, or `kms`). Newly written Secrets are encrypted; to encrypt pre-existing rows, rewrite them (`kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -`). The other three describe fields/flags that don't exist. Notably `--allow-privileged` controls whether pods can request privileged containers; it has no relationship to storage encryption.

questions.question: Your organisation runs HashiCorp Vault. Which integration pattern delivers secrets to pods WITHOUT creating a Kubernetes Secret object at all?
options: Mount a long-lived Vault token as a Kubernetes Secret and let the containerised app use that token to call Vault directly for each secret it needs at runtime
Store the Vault secret values in a ConfigMap annotated `vault.hashicorp.com/encrypt: true`, so the values sit in etcd envelope-encrypted with a Vault-managed key rather than in a Kubernetes Secret
The Vault Agent Injector — a mutating webhook adds a Vault Agent sidecar that authenticates with the pod's SA and writes secrets to a shared in-memory volume

Enable the built-in `secretRef.vault:` field on the pod spec so the kubelet resolves the reference against the cluster-registered Vault provider and writes the value directly into the container's environment
questions.explanation: The Injector's sidecar authenticates to Vault (Kubernetes auth method), fetches secrets, and writes them to a `tmpfs` volume shared with the app — the Kubernetes API never learns the value. (The Vault CSI provider works similarly and is also acceptable, but the sidecar pattern is the one described here.) Storing anything sensitive in a ConfigMap defeats the point; ConfigMaps have no encryption feature of their own. Mounting a static Vault token *does* create a Kubernetes Secret carrying that token — the requirement is not met. There is no in-tree `secretRef.vault` field.

questions.question: Why are Kubernetes Secrets not truly secure by default?
options: Because RBAC rules on the built-in `secrets` resource are advisory in default kubeadm installs and any pod in the namespace can read them until a NetworkPolicy on the metadata endpoint is applied
Because Secret bodies travel from kube-apiserver to etcd over plain HTTP by default and can be sniffed by anyone with control-plane node access until mutual TLS is manually enabled
Because the AES-256 key that protects each Secret lives inside the same etcd database it protects, so anyone with etcd read access can unwrap the value with a single call
Because they are stored in etcd as base64-encoded blobs — base64 is an encoding, not encryption, and trivially reversible
questions.explanation: Without an EncryptionConfiguration, Secrets are stored in etcd as base64 payloads that anyone with etcd disk or backup access can decode with a one-liner. RBAC absolutely applies to Secrets — that is one of the tighter default protections. Communication between kube-apiserver and etcd is TLS by default in kubeadm-installed clusters. There is no default AES-encrypted-with-key-in-etcd flow; the danger is precisely that there is no encryption at all until you opt in.

questions.question: Which Dockerfile pattern yields the smallest, most secure image for a statically-linked Go binary?
options: Multi-stage build: compile in `golang:1.22`, then copy the binary into `FROM scratch` (or `gcr.io/distroless/static`)
`FROM ubuntu:22.04` and `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y golang-go && go build -o /app` in a single layer, using `--no-install-recommends` to keep the image lean
`FROM alpine:latest` with `RUN apk add --no-cache go && go build -ldflags='-s -w' -o /app && apk del go && rm -rf /var/cache/apk/*` to strip the toolchain after building
`FROM golang:1.22-alpine`, `RUN go build -o /app` and set `CMD ["/app"]` — the alpine variant is the smallest official Go image so both compile and runtime share it
questions.explanation: Copying just the binary into `scratch` or `distroless/static` leaves an image with no shell, no package manager, no OS utilities — nothing for an attacker with RCE to pivot with. Ubuntu-based single-stage images ship a full userland (hundreds of MB of attack surface). Alpine with `apk del` still leaves apk metadata, busybox, and shared libraries. `golang:1.22-alpine` bundles the whole Go toolchain into the runtime image — orders of magnitude larger and richer than `scratch`.

questions.question: Which tool statically analyses a Kubernetes resource YAML for security risks and returns an advisory score?
options: `hadolint <manifest.yaml>` — parses the referenced Dockerfile and lints for Docker best practices, warning on missing `USER` directives and unpinned image tags in the manifest
`kubesec scan` — scores a manifest against a fixed set of security rules (privileged, hostPath, missing securityContext, etc.)
`kube-score score <manifest.yaml>` — validates the manifest against the Kubernetes OpenAPI schema and reports schema warnings for missing required fields
`trivy fs --security-checks config <manifest.yaml>` — walks the filesystem containing the manifest and scans image references for CVEs, printing a severity-weighted findings list
questions.explanation: `kubesec` is designed exactly for this: it reads a Pod/Deployment YAML and returns a numeric score plus advisories on privileged, hostPath, capabilities, `runAsNonRoot`, etc. `hadolint` targets Dockerfiles. `trivy fs --security-checks config` does IaC misconfig scans but uses a different rule engine and is not focused on a security *score*. `kube-score` mostly checks operational best practices (probes, resource requests) rather than security posture.

questions.question: Which Cosign subcommand verifies that a container image was signed with a specific public key?
options: `cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0`
`cosign attach signature --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0`
`cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0`
`cosign check --signature cosign.sig registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0`
questions.explanation: `cosign verify --key <pubkey> <image>` fetches the signature artefact stored alongside the image in the OCI registry and validates it against the public key, exiting non-zero on failure. `cosign sign` creates a signature — the opposite operation. `cosign attach` uploads pre-existing artefacts (SBOMs, signatures) but does no verification. `cosign check` does not exist as a subcommand.

questions.question: You want to block pods that pull images from any registry other than `registry.example.com`. Which cluster-wide control fits?
options: Add `imagePullSecrets` in every namespace pointing only to `registry.example.com`
Add a ClusterRole that denies `create` on pods with foreign registry prefixes
Set an environment variable `ALLOWED_REGISTRIES=registry.example.com` on kube-apiserver
Deploy OPA Gatekeeper (or Kyverno) with a ConstraintTemplate that examines each container image prefix
questions.explanation: A policy engine looking at `input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image` at admission time can reject any prefix that doesn't start with the allowed registry. `imagePullSecrets` provide credentials — a pod can still reference `docker.io/x/y` without them and the kubelet will attempt to pull anonymously. There is no such kube-apiserver env var. RBAC evaluates verb/resource combinations only; it cannot inspect a field value like `image`.

questions.question: A platform team picks `gcr.io/distroless/static` as a base for Go services. What is the *primary* security advantage of a distroless base image?
options: It ships with no shell, no package manager, and no debug tools — sharply narrowing what an attacker can do after gaining code execution
It automatically forces the container process to run as a non-root user by hard-coding a non-zero UID in the image, regardless of whether the pod spec sets `runAsUser`
It fetches and applies runtime CVE patches on its own via an embedded update client, so images never have to be rebuilt after a base-image CVE is disclosed
It is signed by the Kubernetes release team with the project's Sigstore key, so admission controllers can skip provenance and image-signature checks for the base layer
questions.explanation: Distroless intentionally strips everything except the runtime dependencies — the attacker gets a functional binary and nothing else to pivot with. Some distroless variants (`static:nonroot`) do default to a non-root UID, but that is variant-specific and the pod spec still overrides. Distroless has no runtime patching mechanism; you rebuild and redeploy. Google-signed image provenance is a separate thing that admission controllers must still verify explicitly — the base image type does not exempt anything.

questions.question: You author a Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate that blocks images whose prefix is not `registry.internal/`. Which Rego shape matches Gatekeeper's contract?
options: `deny[msg] { not startswith(input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image, "registry.internal/"); msg := "image not allowed" }`
`violation[{"msg": msg}] { c := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]; not startswith(c.image, "registry.internal/"); msg := sprintf("image %v not allowed", [c.image]) }`
`deny { every c in input.review.object.spec.containers { not startswith(c.image, "registry.internal/") }; msg := "all containers must come from registry.internal" }`
`block[msg] { image := input.spec.containers[_].image; not contains(image, "registry.internal"); msg := sprintf("blocked image %v", [image]) }`
questions.explanation: Gatekeeper reads `violation[{"msg": msg}]` rules — that fixed name and shape are part of its contract. Neither `deny` nor `block` is a Gatekeeper rule head. Rules that reference `input.spec.containers` also use the wrong input path (Gatekeeper wraps admission review data under `input.review.object`). A `deny` rule with an `every` block cannot emit a per-violation `msg`, so even if `deny` were valid it would not attach the required message field.

questions.question: A mutating admission webhook that injects sidecars goes temporarily unreachable. Which single setting on the `MutatingWebhookConfiguration` prevents that outage from taking down cluster-wide pod creation?
options: `failurePolicy: Fail`
`namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {sidecar-injection: enabled}}`
`failurePolicy: Ignore`
Delete the `MutatingWebhookConfiguration` and rely on the webhook's own health-check recovery
questions.explanation: `Ignore` tells the API server to admit the request without mutation if the webhook cannot be reached — pods still get created (just without the sidecar). `Fail` (the default) blocks admission on webhook errors, which is exactly the failure mode the question wants to avoid. A `namespaceSelector` narrows *which* pods hit the webhook, but any namespace that still targets it will still be blocked. Deleting the configuration removes the sidecar entirely and is not a resilience strategy.

questions.question: You need to scan every running container image in the cluster for HIGH and CRITICAL CVEs with a single Trivy command. Which command works?
options: `trivy image --scan-all-nodes --severity HIGH,CRITICAL`
`trivy cluster --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --output report.html`
`trivy kubernetes --namespace all --severity HIGH,CRITICAL pods`
`trivy k8s --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --report all cluster`
questions.explanation: `trivy k8s cluster` is the cluster-mode scanner. `--report all` prints the full per-workload finding list, and `--severity HIGH,CRITICAL` filters. `trivy image --scan-all-nodes` is fabricated — `trivy image` targets a single image reference. `trivy kubernetes` is not a valid subcommand (the short form `k8s` is used). `trivy cluster` also isn't a subcommand.

questions.question: How do you generate a CycloneDX SBOM for `nginx:1.25` with Trivy?
options: `trivy image --format cyclonedx nginx:1.25`
`trivy image nginx:1.25 --sbom cyclonedx --output sbom.json`
`trivy scan --sbom --format cyclonedx --target nginx:1.25`
`trivy sbom generate --image nginx:1.25 --format cyclonedx`
questions.explanation: `trivy image --format cyclonedx <image>` produces the CycloneDX document (supported formats also include `spdx-json`, `github`, etc.). `--sbom` is not a Trivy flag. `trivy scan` and `trivy sbom generate` are not real subcommands in current Trivy.

questions.question: A Deployment must pull from a private registry. Which pattern authenticates the pull without embedding credentials in the Deployment YAML?
options: Add env vars `REGISTRY_USER` and `REGISTRY_PASSWORD` to the container — kubelet reads them for the pull
Create a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` and reference it via `spec.imagePullSecrets`
Mount a ConfigMap containing `config.json` at `/etc/docker/` inside each container
Drop credentials into `/root/.docker/config.json` on every worker node and let kubelet auto-detect
questions.explanation: That Secret type stores a `.dockerconfigjson` payload and `imagePullSecrets` on the pod (or the SA) points to it — kubelet uses it to authenticate the pull. Container-side env vars are inside the container's process — kubelet, which does the pull, never sees them. A ConfigMap mounted in the container is likewise inaccessible to kubelet's image-pull path. Node-local `/root/.docker/config.json` does work with some kubelets but is node-specific, unversioned, and hard to rotate — the Kubernetes-native pattern is `imagePullSecrets`.

questions.question: Where in a delivery pipeline should container image scanning happen to catch vulnerabilities as early as possible?
options: At admission time — use a validating admission webhook that scans the image and rejects the pod's create request if HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs are present in the layer inventory
Immediately after pushing — configure the registry to trigger a scan on the `image-push` webhook and quarantine the tag if HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs are found
Before pushing to the registry — scan the locally built image and fail the build if HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs are found
Continuously at runtime — schedule a CronJob that runs `trivy k8s cluster` on every namespace hourly and posts findings to the ticketing system
questions.explanation: Shift-left: the earliest safe point is CI, right after build and before push. A vulnerable image never enters the registry, never reaches admission, never runs. Post-push scanning still allows the image to sit in the registry and be pulled while the scan is queued. Admission-time scanning is a valuable last line of defence but reacts very late. Continuous runtime scanning is a monitoring pattern — vulnerabilities are already running by the time it flags them.

questions.question: You configure an `ImagePolicyWebhook` with `defaultAllow: false`. The external webhook server goes down. What happens to new pod admission requests?
options: The API server caches the last decision and continues to admit or reject as before
Only pods in `kube-system` are allowed through; everything else is blocked
Kubernetes falls back to allowing every image (fail-open)
All pod admission requests are denied until the webhook is available again (fail-closed)
questions.explanation: `defaultAllow: false` is the fail-closed mode: no reachable scanner means no admissions. The opposite value, `defaultAllow: true`, would fail open and admit everything during an outage — the insecure choice for a policy control. The ImagePolicyWebhook has no built-in result cache and no namespace-based fallback.

questions.question: Which Falco condition alerts whenever any process inside a container reads `/etc/shadow`?
options: `open_read and container and fd.name=/etc/shadow`
`syscall.type=read and file.path=/etc/shadow and kubernetes.namespace != ""`
`read_file and container and filename contains "/etc/shadow"`
`evt.type=openat and container.id != "" and path.file="/etc/shadow"`
questions.explanation: The `open_read` macro matches read-mode file opens; the `container` macro scopes to container context; `fd.name` is the full file path field. Together they express the intent cleanly. Options A/C/D reference fields and macros Falco doesn't have — `file.path`, `read_file`, `filename`, `path.file`, and `kubernetes.namespace` are not part of Falco's field/macro set (the closest real ones are `fd.name` and `k8s.ns.name`).

questions.question: Your audit log is drowning in ConfigMap `get`/`list`/`watch` noise. How do you suppress just those events?
options: Set the `configmaps` API group to `Ignore` in the audit-backend webhook config so the audit webhook silently drops those events before they reach the backend
Prepend a rule `level: None; verbs: ["get","list","watch"]; resources: [{group: "", resources: ["configmaps"]}]` BEFORE any broader-scope rules in the audit policy
Add `omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]` globally to the audit policy so ConfigMap get/list/watch events are dropped at the pre-response stage and never persisted
Append the same `level: None` rule at the END of the audit policy so, as the last-declared rule, it acts as a final override on any earlier match for ConfigMap reads
questions.explanation: Audit policy rules are first-match-wins, top-to-bottom. Place the `None` rule for ConfigMap reads at the top so it matches before any wider `Metadata`/`RequestResponse` rule catches those events. Appending it at the end never takes effect — earlier rules already matched. `omitStages: RequestReceived` only drops that one stage of an event; the completion stage is still emitted. Audit backends don't have per-resource ignore settings.

questions.question: Which combination best implements the immutable-infrastructure model for a Kubernetes workload?
options: Allow writable root filesystems but keep `/var/log` read-only, push new code with `kubectl cp` into running pods, and restart containers rather than replacing them
Disable all image registries and have each node clone the repo and rebuild the binary at pod startup
Set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, bake all code and dependencies into the image at build time, and roll out new versions by replacing pods (rolling or canary)
Mount `/opt` as a hostPath read-write so operators can patch binaries directly on hosts during incidents
questions.explanation: Immutable infrastructure means the runtime artefact is not mutated in place — the image is the unit of change, root FS is read-only, and deploys replace pods rather than editing them. Copying files into a running container is the definition of a mutable-runtime approach. Building at pod startup violates immutability and reproducibility (and drags in a network of build-time risks). hostPath patching bypasses image-based delivery entirely.

questions.question: You run Falco as a DaemonSet and want alerts pushed to Slack in real time without writing any code. What is the standard mechanism?
options: Disable the syscall driver and schedule a CronJob that re-runs Falco offline against historical logs, posting summaries to Slack
Patch Falco to embed a Slack webhook URL in its main source
Set `outputs.rate: 0` and rely on Kubernetes events; the K8s event stream propagates to Slack automatically
Run Falcosidekick alongside Falco and configure its Slack webhook output; Falco streams events to Falcosidekick over HTTP or gRPC
questions.explanation: Falcosidekick is the community-standard fan-out for Falco events — Slack, Teams, PagerDuty, Elasticsearch, S3, and many others via config. Falco itself has no built-in Slack output — patching is an anti-pattern and unnecessary. Kubernetes events do not propagate to Slack on their own. Falco's power is its live syscall driver; running it offline against logs would miss the entire runtime signal.

questions.question: You want to stream Kubernetes audit events to an external SIEM in near real time. Which built-in audit backend fits?
options: The webhook backend — kube-apiserver POSTs audit events to an HTTP endpoint you configure with `--audit-webhook-config-file`
The dynamic backend, enabled with `--audit-dynamic-configuration=true` — an AuditSink CR then routes events to any HTTP endpoint that can serve as a SIEM receiver
The Kafka backend, enabled with `--audit-kafka-config=/etc/kubernetes/audit-kafka.yaml` — kube-apiserver publishes each event straight to the configured Kafka topic
The log backend (`--audit-log-path=/var/log/audit.log`) — kube-apiserver writes JSON events to the file and a node-local shipper such as Fluent Bit tails it to the SIEM
questions.explanation: The webhook backend is the near-real-time option: batched POSTs of audit events to your SIEM's collector or a forwarder. The dynamic audit config was removed in Kubernetes 1.27. There is no in-tree Kafka backend for audit — Kafka integration is external (e.g., through the webhook backend feeding a Kafka producer). The log backend works but is file-based and pulls latency through whatever tails it; the webhook is the more direct streaming path.

questions.question: Which Falco condition best detects an interactive shell being spawned inside a container, e.g. after `kubectl exec … -- bash`?
options: `evt.type = open and fd.name startswith /etc/passwd and container.id != ""` — matches reads of `/etc/passwd` inside a container, which is a technique used by shell probes to enumerate users
`spawned_process and container and proc.name in (bash, sh, zsh, ksh, dash) and not proc.pname in (runc, containerd)`
`container.image.repository contains alpine and spawned_process` — flags any process spawned inside an alpine-based container, where alpine's minimal base image is the common shell playground
`k8s.ns.name = kube-system and proc.name = kubelet and evt.type = execve` — narrows the alert to kubelet-triggered process launches inside the control-plane namespace
questions.explanation: `spawned_process` catches `execve`; the `container` macro scopes to container context; the process-name list matches common shells, and the negative parent-name filter reduces false positives from the container runtime's own startup shell. Rules that watch `evt.type=open` on `/etc/passwd` monitor file reads — a different technique that misses the exec itself. Filtering by `container.image.repository` alone fires on every workload start, generating pure noise with no behavioural signal. Matching `kubelet` inside `kube-system` alerts on expected kubelet activity, not on shell spawns.

questions.question: After a Secret in the `prod` namespace was deleted maliciously, which audit-log fields let you attribute the action to a specific user and object?
options: `event.source.component`, `event.requestURI`, and `event.verb`
`annotations.authorization.k8s.io/reason`, `userAgent`, and `responseStatus.code`
`user.username`, `verb`, `objectRef.namespace`, `objectRef.resource`, `objectRef.name`
`auditID`, `sourceIPs`, and `requestReceivedTimestamp`
questions.explanation: Together these fields identify *who* did *what* to *which* object *where*. The authorization-reason annotation only explains why the decision was allowed/denied. `userAgent` and `responseStatus.code` describe the client and the HTTP status, not the actor identity. `auditID`, `sourceIPs`, `requestReceivedTimestamp` are useful correlation metadata but don't name the user or the deleted Secret.

questions.question: During incident response the SRE lead replaces a compromised pod with a freshly pulled image rather than exec-ing in to clean it. Their images are truly immutable (read-only rootfs, no shell, no package manager). What is the key runtime-security benefit of that immutability for IR?
options: Immutability prevents in-pod attackers from mutating cluster resources such as NetworkPolicy objects, since the container's SA has no write access and the root FS blocks kubectl download
Immutable containers self-restart every 24 h via a built-in lifecycle timer so any attacker foothold in memory is wiped daily without operator intervention
Immutability makes the host kernel image itself read-only via a runtime hook, blocking kernel-module rootkits on the node the compromised container is scheduled on
Any observed filesystem write on the container is definitionally attacker behaviour, which sharpens detection and eliminates most false positives
questions.explanation: With `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` and no in-place install paths, the app can't legitimately modify its own root FS — so any write event surfaced by Falco/eBPF is a real signal, not application noise. NetworkPolicy is a cluster-side API object; nothing about pod immutability protects it (RBAC does). Immutable containers don't auto-restart on a fixed schedule. Container immutability is a userland construct — it doesn't change kernel writability on the node.

questions.question: Attackers are reading `/proc/1/environ` inside containers to harvest credentials that were passed to the pod as environment variables. Which change most directly stops that class of leak?
options: Stop putting credentials in the pod's `env:` block; deliver them as file mounts from Secrets (or via a secrets-manager sidecar / CSI) so they never appear in the process environment
Set `hostPID: true` cluster-wide so the pod's `/proc` view merges with the host's — a unified PID namespace lets an admission control filter see and reject `/proc/1/environ` reads centrally
Add a NetworkPolicy that denies all egress from the pod so any credentials that do end up in the environment cannot be exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled destination
Switch the container runtime from containerd to CRI-O — CRI-O's default profile masks `/proc/<pid>/environ` for non-init processes, while containerd exposes it to the container root user
questions.explanation: Once a value is in the process environment, `/proc/<pid>/environ` reveals it to anyone with read access on the pod — including an attacker with RCE. Mounting the Secret as a file with restrictive perms (or fetching at runtime via Vault Agent/CSI) keeps the value out of the environment block entirely. `hostPID: true` broadens process visibility across the host rather than restricting it. An egress deny stops exfiltration but doesn't stop the local read of `environ`. Both containerd and CRI-O expose `environ` identically — swapping runtimes doesn't affect this leak.

questions.question: A container has been flagged for runtime compromise. You must capture its filesystem for forensics with minimum interference to the live pod. Which approach is safest?
options: `kubectl cp <pod>:/ /forensics/` to pull a live copy of the container filesystem — the cp command runs `tar` inside the container to stream the bytes, so it works even without shell access
SSH to the node and use `crictl inspect` / `ctr` to locate the container's overlay layers under the runtime state dir and snapshot them from the host
`kubectl exec <pod> -- tar -czf /tmp/rootfs.tar.gz /` and then `kubectl cp` the archive out — captures files exactly as the compromised container sees them, including any masked mounts
`kubectl debug --copy-to=<pod>-debug <pod>` to spin up a clone of the pod with the same volumes, then run forensic tooling in the sidecar without touching the original process
questions.explanation: Working from the node lets you capture the overlay layers without executing anything inside the potentially-instrumented container — no attacker tooling runs, no evidence is disturbed. `kubectl cp` invokes `tar` inside the container, which runs attacker-influenced binaries. `kubectl exec … tar` is even more invasive — the attacker's tooling can trap `tar` and modify what gets emitted. `kubectl debug --copy-to` creates a new pod from the same PodSpec — useful for reproducing behaviour, but the *original* is what carries the evidence.

questions.question: Your audit policy currently records Secrets at `RequestResponse`, which puts base64 Secret values into the audit log. You want to keep an audit trail of *who* accessed which Secret without recording the values themselves. Which policy change does that?
options: Set `level: None` for the `secrets` resource so no audit event is generated for read or write operations on any Secret in the cluster
Set `level: Request` for Secrets — captures the write body but drops the response
Set `level: Metadata` for Secrets — logs user, verb, timestamp, and object reference, without any request/response body
Add a redaction admission webhook that scrubs the `data` and `stringData` fields from every Secret request before the audit backend sees the event
questions.explanation: `Metadata` is the exact level for who/when/what without payload. `None` drops everything — no trail at all. `Request` still logs write bodies, and for reads the sensitive data is in the response, which is still captured at `RequestResponse` — Metadata is the level that omits both. Kubernetes audit logging has no built-in redaction; a webhook cannot rewrite events after the API server emits them.

questions.question: A `RuntimeClass` named `gvisor` targets the `runsc` handler. You want every pod in the `untrusted` namespace to *automatically* use it without editing each pod spec. Which mechanism does that?
options: Annotate the namespace `scheduler.alpha.kubernetes.io/runtimeClass=gvisor` — the namespace-annotation-defaults controller propagates the value into every new pod spec's `runtimeClassName` field
Reference the RuntimeClass from a LimitRange object in the namespace so LimitRange's default-injection mechanism sets `spec.runtimeClassName` on every new pod that omits it
Create a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration on pod-create in `untrusted` that admits pods whose `runtimeClassName` is `gvisor` and rewrites any other value or absence to `gvisor` inline
Add a MutatingAdmissionWebhook (or a Kyverno mutation ClusterPolicy / a Gatekeeper mutation) that injects `spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor` at admission
questions.explanation: Only a *mutating* admission step can add fields to the incoming pod spec. Namespace annotations are metadata — they don't propagate into child objects' fields. LimitRange caps resource requests/limits, nothing about runtime handlers. A ValidatingWebhookConfiguration can reject pods that lack the field, but it never fills it in — the user still has to author it correctly.

questions.question: A team wants to reduce the blast radius of code that gains RCE inside a container. Which TWO Pod-level settings most directly shrink the blast radius?
options: `securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true`
`securityContext.privileged: true` — grants the container near-host capabilities and disables Linux namespace isolation
`securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`
`hostNetwork: true` — attaches the pod directly to the node's network namespace so it can see and dial every listening port on the host
questions.explanation: Running as a non-root UID means the exploited process cannot use root-only kernel paths, and dropping every Linux capability strips the process of privileged operations (raw sockets, kernel module load, etc.) even if it lands on a root UID. `privileged: true` grants near-host access — it *widens* the blast radius. `hostNetwork: true` joins the host's network namespace, exposing every service on the node to the compromised process — again the opposite of containment.
